== History ==
The shrine was established by transfer (kanjō) from {{ill|Taga-taisha|el|Τάγκα-τάισα|fr|Taga-taisha|ja|多賀大社|tr|Taga-taisha|zh|多賀大社|qid=Q402091}} in {{ill|Ōmi Province|ca|Província d'Ōmi|ckb|پارێزگای ئۆمی|cs|Provincie Ómi|de|Provinz Ōmi|es|Provincia de Ōmi|fa|ولایت اومی|fi|Ōmin provinssi|fr|Province d'Ōmi|gl|Provincia de Ōmi|hak|Ōmi-koet|id|Provinsi Ōmi|it|Ōmi|ja|近江国|ko|오미국|lt|Omio žemė|nl|Omi (provincie)|pl|Prowincja Ōmi|pt|Província de Ōmi|ru|Оми (провинция)|simple|Ōmi Province|sk|Ómi (provincia)|sr|Провинција Оми|tr|Ōmi (vilayet)|uk|Провінція Омі|vi|Tỉnh Ōmi|zh|近江國|zh_min_nan|Ômi-kok|zh_yue|近江國|qid=Q843882}}. In {{ill|Enryaku|de|Enryaku|es|Enryaku|fa|انریاکو|fr|Ère Enryaku|ia|Enryaku|id|Enryaku|it|Enryaku|ja|延暦|ko|엔랴쿠|pt|Enryaku|ru|Энряку (нэнго)|simple|Enryaku|sr|Енрјаку|tr|Enryaku|uk|Енряку (ненґо)|zh|延曆|zh_yue|延曆|qid=Q1373176}} 15 ({{ill|796|ab|796|af|796|am|796 እ.ኤ.አ.|an|796|ar|796|ary|796|arz|796|ast|796|avk|796|az|796|azb|۷۹۶ (میلادی)|bcl|796|be|796|be_x_old|796|bg|796|bn|৭৯৬|bpy|মারি ৭৯৬|br|796|bs|796.|ca|796|cdo|796 nièng|ceb|796|ckb|٧٩٦|crh|796|cs|796|cv|796|cy|796|da|796|de|796|el|796|eml|796|eo|796|es|796|et|796|eu|796|fa|۷۹۶ (میلادی)|fi|796|fo|796|fr|796|frr|796|fy|796|ga|796|gan|796年|gd|796|gl|796|he|796|hi|796|hr|796.|ht|796 (almanak jilyen)|hu|796|hy|796|id|796|io|796|is|796|it|796|ja|796年|jv|796|ka|796|kaa|796|kk|796 жыл|ko|796년|la|796|lb|796|lij|796|lmo|796|lt|796 m.|lv|796. gads|map_bms|796|mdf|796|mg|796|mhr|796|mk|796|mr|इ.स. ७९६|mrj|796 и|ms|796|mzn|۷۹۶|nah|796|nap|796|nds|796|new|सन् ७९६|nl|796|nn|796|no|796|nrm|796|nso|796|oc|796|or|୭୯୬|os|796-æм аз|pl|796|pnb|796|pt|796|qu|796|ro|796|ru|796 год|rue|796|sa|७९६|sah|796|scn|796|sd|796ع|sh|796.|shn|796|si|796|sk|796|sl|796|sq|796|sr|796|su|796|sv|796|sw|796|tg|Соли 796|th|พ.ศ. 1339|tk|796|tl|796|tly|796|tr|796|tt|796 ел|uk|796|ur|796ء|uz|796|vec|796|vi|796|war|796|wuu|796年|xmf|796|zh|796年|zh_min_nan|796 nî|zh_yue|796年|qid=Q33452}}), it received the divine rank of {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade}} from the {{ill|Imperial Court of Japan|ja|朝廷 (日本)|qid=Q30253177}}. Later, as {{ill|Taga Castle|ca|Castell de Taga|cs|Hrad Taga|de|Burg Taga|es|Castillo de Taga|fa|قلعه تاگا|fr|Site de Tagajō|ja|多賀城|ko|타가성|ml|ടാഗ കാസിൽ|ru|Тага (замок)|uk|Замок Таґа|zh|多賀城|qid=Q870867}} declined, the shrine also fell into decline and its location became unknown. At Shiogama Shrine, the Ichinomiya of {{ill|Mutsu Province|ca|Província de Mutsu|cs|Provincie Mucu|de|Provinz Mutsu|es|Provincia de Mutsu|fa|ولایت موتسو|fi|Mutsun provinssi|fr|Province de Mutsu|gl|Provincia de Mutsu|id|Provinsi Mutsu|it|Mutsu (provincia)|ja|陸奥国|ko|무쓰국|lt|Mucu žemė|nl|Mutsu (provincie)|pt|Província de Mutsu|ru|Муцу (провинция)|simple|Mutsu Province|sk|Mucu (provincia)|sr|Провинција Муцу|tr|Mutsu (vilayet)|uk|Муцу (провінція)|zh|陸奧國|zh_classical|陸奧國|zh_min_nan|Mutu-kok|zh_yue|陸奧國|qid=Q907389}}, the 1745 record “Shiogama Shaki” ({{ill|Enkyō (Edo period)|de|Enkyō|fa|انکیو (دوره ادو)|fr|Ère Enkyō (Edo)|it|Enkyō (periodo Edo)|ja|延享|ko|엔쿄 (에도 시대)|ru|Энкё (Эдо)|simple|Enkyō (Edo period)|sr|Енкјо (Едо период)|sv|Enkyō|tr|Enkyō (Edo)|zh|延享|qid=Q1183728}} 2) speculated that the foundation stones at “Tō-no-koshihara,” where the pagoda ruins of the former Tagajō temple now stand, were the remains of the ancient grand shrine “Taga Shrine.”

The village tutelary shrine “Shinmei-sha,” located in the hamlet “Tō-no-koshi” of Takasaki Village, is described in the “Fudoki Goyōshodashi” (An’ei 3 [1774], Takasaki Village) as having an unknown origin of enshrinement, with no mention of any connection to “Taga Shrine.” Instead, for “Tō-no-koshihara,” it records a tradition that “there once stood a seven-hall temple complex with a five-story pagoda,” and notes that “even now the stone foundations remain exposed.” The hamlet names for Shinmei-sha and the temple ruin foundation stones differ, and although their locations are adjacent, they appear to have been slightly offset. At the Taga Shrine in Rokugatsuzaka, located almost directly north of the main hall of the Tagajō government complex, many bamboo hoops (taga) woven from bamboo—like those dedicated at the head shrine {{ill|Taga-taisha|el|Τάγκα-τάισα|fr|Taga-taisha|ja|多賀大社|tr|Taga-taisha|zh|多賀大社|qid=Q402091}}, which enshrines {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Izanagi}} and {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Izanami}}—have been offered.<ref>According to Tōshirō Shimizu, “Tagajō Ruins,” in *Miyagi Prefecture Historic Sites, Scenic Places, and Natural Monuments Survey Report*, Vol. 3, Miyagi Prefecture Historic Sites, Scenic Places, and Natural Monuments Survey Committee, Shōwa 2 (1927), pp. 41–134, in the section “Legends of Various Places within Tagajō” (Kikuchi Mitsuya, pp. 128–131), it states: “Taga Shrine lies north of the inner fortress, beside the old Shiogama road. Villagers string together bamboo hoops equal in number to their age and hang them before the shrine to pray for longevity. Behind this small shrine, the foundation stones of the former shrine buildings are scattered, and several large stones excavated nearby are all massive. It is said that the former shrine buildings were grand and magnificent. The fields behind the shrine are said to be the sites of ancient halls, and even now they are cultivated without fertilization. In a corner of the temple ruins at Takasaki, on the pagoda platform, there is a Taga Shrine, but it was moved from here; before this shrine there are no hoop offerings, and villagers commonly refer to it as ‘Oise-sama.’”</ref> At present, the Tagajō City Board of Education officially recognizes this as the “Engishiki Shrine: Taga Shrine,” and has installed official markers and information boards. The former shrine site lies about 50 meters northeast of the current location, and through excavation surveys and environmental improvement projects in the Rokugatsuzaka area, the shrine was {{ill|Sengū|de|Sengū|ja|遷宮|qid=Q2271023}} to its present site. Before relocation, a {{ill|Torii|ar|توري|az|Torii|bcl|Torii|bg|Тории|ca|Torii|cs|Torii|de|Torii|el|Τορίι|eo|Torijo|es|Torii|et|Torii|eu|Torii|fa|توریئی|fi|Torii|fr|Torii|he|טוריאי|hu|Torii|hy|Տորիի|id|Torii|it|Torii|ja|鳥居|jv|Torii|ko|도리이|lt|Torii|ms|Torii|nl|Torii|no|Torii|oc|Torii|pl|Torii|pt|Torii|ru|Тории|simple|Torii|sl|Tori|sq|Torii|sv|Torii|ta|தொரீ|th|โทริอิ|tr|Torii|uk|Торії|uz|Torii|vi|Torii|wuu|鳥居|zh|鳥居|qid=Q234731}} gate was also in place, but it no longer exists. In the “An’ei Fudoki Shodashi” (An’ei 3 [1774]) of Ichikawa Village, only four shrines—the village tutelary Sōsha Myōjin Shrine (present-day {{ill|Mutsu Sōsha-no-miya|ja|陸奥総社宮|qid=Q11658605}}), Arahaba-ki Shrine, Hakusan Shrine, and Hachiman Shrine—are listed; this shrine is not mentioned, and details of its shrine traditions remain unknown.
